name: viewer-frame
description:
A pane that shows content it did not author — a rendered artifact, a document preview, a diff. The app has three of these and they share the problem: the content inside is arbitrary, so the frame has to survive anything, and the frame is the only part this system controls.

The rule it carries is that arbitrary content gets its OWN scroll container and never the page's. A viewer that grows to its content pushes the toolbar off the top and takes the app shell's layout with it — which is the same `min-block-size: 0` failure as the shell, one level down.

base.$description:
CONTAINER. This unit establishes an inline-size container named after itself, so anything inside it can respond to the width of THIS BOX rather than to the width of the window. That is the difference that matters for a design system: a composite dropped into a 320px sidebar and the same composite on a 320px phone are the same situation, and a viewport query calls them different ones. The library carries no viewport media query anywhere for exactly this reason — the only `@media` in it is `prefers-reduced-motion`, which is a person's setting and not a size.

`inline-size: 100%` is the container's REQUIRED companion, not a preference. `container-type: inline-size` makes the box's width independent of its contents — that is the containment being asked for — so a container with no width of its own has nothing left to size from and collapses to zero. This unit did: centred in a grid it became a column of single words. A container fills what it is given and bounds itself with `max-inline-size`; it never sizes to its text.

toolbar.$description: Fixed at the top of the frame, never scrolling with the content. `flex-shrink: 0` is what holds it there — without it a tall content pane squeezes the toolbar to nothing rather than scrolling.

content.$description: Its own scroll, and `min-block-size: 0` so it actually shrinks. Arbitrary content also means arbitrary width, so `overflow: auto` on both axes — a wide table or a long code line scrolls INSIDE the frame rather than widening the app.
What kind of thing is inside, which decides the padding and the type.

code.$description: Monospace, no wrap, tabular. A code viewer that wraps loses the line structure the reader is there for.

media.$description: Edge to edge and centred. Padding around a rendered image is padding around the only thing in the frame.

a11y.note: The scrolling region carries `tabindex="0"` and a label — a scrollable area that cannot be focused cannot be scrolled by keyboard, which is WCAG 2.1.1 and the most common failure in any viewer. The label says what is inside, not that it is a viewer. Content the frame did not author must not be trusted to be accessible: the frame guarantees the container, not the contents, and that boundary should be stated wherever this is used for third-party output.
